title: Sudama's flattened rice
hookLine: a poor man visits his richest friend, forgets to ask for anything, and walks home happy anyway
carry: God receives the love, not the size
tomorrow: why does the kirtan's first song go to Ganesha?

lines: A POOR MAN AT THE GATES.
cards: A thin man in a torn cloth stands at the gates of Dwaraka, holding a small bundle. He's a brahmin, poor enough that his family often goes hungry.
His wife sent him: go to your old friend, the one you studied with as a boy. He's the lord of Dwaraka now. Surely he'll help.
The man didn't want to ask. He came mostly to see his friend's face. In the bundle is the only gift his house could find: a few handfuls of flattened rice, begged from the neighbors.

teach.b: Krishna sees him from across the palace, leaves his seat beside Rukmini, runs to him, and embraces him. He washes his friend's feet.
They talk about their school days at Sandipani's house, and the night a storm caught them gathering firewood, holding hands in the dark until their teacher found them at dawn and blessed them.
Then Krishna asks, smiling: what did you bring me? The brahmin is too ashamed to show it.
So Krishna takes the bundle himself and eats a handful of the rice with delight. As he reaches for more, Rukmini gently catches his hand, as if to say: that's enough.
That one handful is plenty for everything your friend will ever need. In the morning he walks home.
He never asked. Krishna never offered. And he goes happy, thinking, in paraphrase: he didn't give me wealth, so that I wouldn't become proud and forget him.
He reaches his village and can't find his hut. In its place is a house shining like a palace, and his wife comes out to meet him.
The Bhagavata gives him a last reflection: Krishna gives a great deal and counts it as little, and takes a small thing from his devotee and counts it as a great deal.

teach.h: A LEAF, A FLOWER, WITH LOVE.
teach.b: In the Gita, Krishna says it outright: a leaf, a flower, a fruit, a little water, offered with love, I accept. That's why Hindus offer God food, flowers and water every day, and share it back as prasad.
What God receives is the love, not the size. The brahmin lives on in that house, his heart where it was. On Krishna.

how: Hindus tell the story of Sudama, also called Kuchela in South India, as a picture of friendship with God, and in some places devotees offer flattened rice to Krishna in memory of it.

o: a rich merchant who gave Krishna a palace of gold
Krishna's poor boyhood friend, who brought flattened rice
Krishna's teacher, who asked for his lost son back

games.q: the poor brahmin's visit — tap the pairs.
p: a house shining like a palace

s: the brahmin asks Krishna for help with his poverty
he never asks, and walks home happy anyway.
Krishna and the brahmin studied together at Sandipani's house
they remember a stormy night in the forest gathering firewood for the teacher's wife.
Krishna politely sets the rice aside
he takes the bundle himself and eats a handful with delight.

games.q: your family is visiting the temple and all you have to offer is one banana. by Sudama's story, what fits?
o: skip it. one banana looks cheap.
offer it gladly. what's received is the love.
wait until you can bring a full tray.
games.why: Krishna took Sudama's handful of rice himself and ate it with delight. in the Gita he accepts even a leaf or a little water given with love.

practice: Take one small thing near you: a glass of water, a piece of fruit, a flower from outside. Hold it a moment the way the brahmin held his bundle.

If you pray, set it before an image or simply lift it and say a name you love, then eat or drink it as prasad; if you don't, give it in your mind to someone you love, and let the gladness of giving be enough.

wordCard.voice: Sudama, the poor brahmin and Krishna's boyhood friend. Today, his flattened rice, and a God who counts a small gift, given with love, as a great one.

carryVoice: Your line: God receives the love, not the size. A handful of rice, eaten with delight. That's day nine hundred eighty-six.
